speaker: Patrick Collison
question: In biomedical research, what makes programmable biology newly plausible for tackling complex diseases?
guest: What I didn't appreciate until spending more time in biology is that humanity has never cured a complex disease. After infectious diseases and monogenic diseases, complex diseases—most cardiovascular disease, cancers, autoimmune, and neurodegenerative diseases—are the residual where we may have treatments that help, like statins, but we don't understand the causal pathways well enough to cure them. That's partly because we haven't had experimental and epistemic technology up to the task: gene pleiotropy across cellular systems creates huge combinatoric complexity, compounded by vast, hard-to-quantify environmental factors. Over the last ten years, though, we've gotten three new classes of technology in biology. For reading, we've gotten much better sequencing, especially single-cell RNA sequencing. At the thinking level, we've gotten deep learning and transformers. And on the writing side, we've seen huge improvements in functional genomics, CRISPR, and bridge editing—the ability to make very specific directed perturbations in cells. Put those together, and at the level of the individual cell you now have the ability to read, think, and write, which starts to feel like a new kind of Turing loop with its own completeness.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Programmable biology has become plausible because three capabilities matured at the same time and now reinforce one another.

First, we can read biology at scale: cheap sequencing, single-cell and spatial omics, and large perturbation screens reveal how complex diseases arise from networks of genes and cell states, not single faults.

Second, we can write and edit it with precision. CRISPR-based tools (base, prime and epigenetic editing), mRNA and lipid nanoparticle delivery, engineered cell therapies such as CAR-T, and synthetic gene circuits let researchers treat cells and molecules as designable systems. Many of these are modular platforms, where changing a guide RNA or sequence retargets the therapy without reinventing it.

Third, AI can now model and design biology. Protein structure prediction and generative design (AlphaFold, RFdiffusion), along with foundation models trained on genomic and cellular data, make it possible to predict the effects of interventions and design new molecules computationally.

Together with automated, high-throughput labs, these create a fast design-build-test-learn loop. That matters for complex diseases such as cancer, autoimmunity and neurodegeneration, which require multi-target, context-sensing interventions rather than single-target drugs.

models.answer:
Complex diseases such as cancer, neurodegeneration, and autoimmunity arise not from single broken genes, but from dysregulated networks spanning dynamic cell states and tissue microenvironments. Programmable biology has become newly plausible for tackling them because capabilities for reading, modeling, writing, and delivering biological instructions have converged into an iterative engineering loop.

Single-cell and spatial multi-omics, combined with high-throughput perturbation screens, now map causal disease circuits at cellular resolution rather than bulk averages. Biological foundation models and generative AI translate those massive datasets into predictive models of cell behavior, enabling the *de novo* design of proteins, regulatory switches, and synthetic gene circuits. Meanwhile, modular effectors—including multiplexed CRISPR, base, prime, and epigenome editors, programmable RNAs, and logic-gated engineered cells—can sense local disease cues and modulate multiple pathways conditionally rather than hitting one static target. Paired with tissue-selective lipid nanoparticles, engineered viral capsids, and automated lab-in-the-loop experimentation, these advances allow researchers to test, refine, and deploy interventions that actively steer complex cellular networks back toward health.

Unlike single-gene disorders, complex conditions like cancer, autoimmunity, and neurodegeneration arise from dynamic regulatory networks and shifting microenvironments that resist conventional, single-target drugs. Today, single-cell and spatial multi-omics map these diseased states in fine detail, revealing exact cellular signatures and network vulnerabilities. Simultaneously, biological foundation models can interpret these vast datasets to design custom proteins, synthetic gene circuits, and conditional RNA switches, turning therapeutic discovery from trial-and-error screening into rational engineering. Equally important, breakthroughs in writing and delivering biological instructions—such as multiplexable base, prime, and epigenetic editors, engineered cells equipped with molecular logic gates, and tissue-targeted lipid nanoparticles or viral capsids—enable multi-pathway interventions in specific cells without broad toxicity. Paired with automated, high-throughput experiments that rapidly validate and refine designs, these advances allow researchers to build therapeutics that sense complex disease cues and mount coordinated, adaptive responses inside the body.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Programmable biology is newly plausible because several technologies have matured at the same time and now work together as an engineering loop: design, build, test, learn.

On the "read" side, single-cell and spatial multi-omics now produce detailed maps of the cell states and gene networks behind complex diseases such as cancer, autoimmunity and neurodegeneration. These diseases involve many genes and depend on context, so they can't be explained by one faulty gene. On the "write" side, precise editing tools (CRISPR, base editing and prime editing), cheap DNA synthesis, and better delivery methods (lipid nanoparticles, engineered viral vectors) let researchers change cells in deliberate, targeted ways. Pooled CRISPR screens linked to single-cell readouts, such as Perturb-seq, test thousands of changes at once and show cause and effect rather than just correlation. AI models trained on this data can predict protein structures, design new proteins, and simulate how cells respond to a change.

Together, these let researchers design multi-part treatments, such as logic-gated CAR-T cells, gene circuits and engineered proteins. These can sense several disease signals at once, so they can act on whole networks rather than single targets.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Programmable biology has become newly plausible for tackling complex diseases because several previously separate capabilities are now converging into a reliable engineering stack. First, artificial intelligence trained on massive genomic, structural, and single-cell multi-omic datasets can now predict how biological systems behave and generate custom proteins, regulatory sequences, and therapeutic RNAs on demand, replacing slow trial-and-error with rational design. Second, precision molecular tools—including base, prime, and epigenetic editors alongside synthetic gene circuits—allow researchers to modify multiple genetic pathways at once and program cells to sense local disease cues, acting only in specific tissues or cell states. That conditional control is essential for multifactorial conditions like cancer, autoimmunity, and neurodegeneration, where blunt, single-target drugs often fail or cause toxicity. Finally, improved delivery systems such as targeted lipid nanoparticles, paired with automated high-throughput biofoundries, rapidly close the design-build-test-learn loop, enabling scientists to iterate on living medicines at a speed and scale that was previously impossible.

noweb.answer: Programmable biology has become newly plausible for complex diseases because advances in artificial intelligence, precision molecular engineering, and high-throughput experimentation have converged into closed design-build-test cycles. Modern biological foundation models can now predict protein structures, gene regulation, and cellular responses to perturbations, enabling researchers to design new molecules and regulatory circuits computationally rather than relying solely on trial and error. At the same time, tools such as CRISPR base and prime editors, epigenetic modulators, programmable RNA therapeutics, and engineered cell therapies allow precise, multi-target, and context-dependent interventions. Crucially, single-cell multi-omics, pooled perturbation screens, and lab automation generate the large-scale, high-resolution data needed to train these models and validate designs rapidly. Because complex diseases like cancer, neurodegeneration, and autoimmune disorders arise from interacting genetic, cellular, and environmental networks rather than single defective genes, the ability to engineer therapies that sense disease states and coordinate nuanced, multi-pathway responses makes tackling them far more achievable.

Programmable biology is newly plausible because researchers can now measure what goes wrong in individual cells, design interventions that change how those cells behave, and test the results at scale. Single-cell and spatial profiling reveal which cells are affected and how they interact. Gene editing, RNA medicines, and engineered cell therapies give researchers ways to alter those behaviors. High-throughput experiments and machine learning help them decide which changes to try and learn from the results.

That combination matters for diseases like cancer and autoimmune disorders, where several mechanisms may interact and differ across patients. A therapy could respond to signals in a particular cell or tissue, or influence several pathways together. The tools make those ideas testable. The hard part is delivering the therapy to the right cells and showing that it works safely and reliably in patients.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Programmable biology is becoming plausible because researchers can increasingly measure what goes wrong in individual cells, design a targeted change, and test whether it helps. Single-cell sequencing reveals disease-related differences that can disappear when researchers average measurements across a tissue. Computational models help identify promising targets, and tools such as CRISPR let researchers test whether changing a gene’s activity actually alters disease behavior.

For complex diseases, the promise extends beyond editing a single gene. Researchers can engineer cells to respond to combinations of molecular signals. An immune cell, for example, can be designed to attack only when it detects a particular combination of tumor markers, which could help it spare healthy tissue that shares one marker. The ability to build and test such conditional responses makes therapies that account for disease complexity increasingly realistic, though delivering them safely and reliably remains a challenge.
